statement: A state-space model represents a system by a state vector x whose first-order (differential or difference) dynamics, together with an output map, describe the system's behavior. General (possibly nonlinear, time-varying) form: ẋ(t) = f(t, x(t), u(t)) [state equation], y(t) = h(t, x(t), u(t)) [output equation]. When f is a linear combination of states and inputs (linear, time-invariant, finite-dimensional case), this reduces to matrix form: ẋ(t) = A x(t) + B u(t), y(t) = C x(t) + D u(t).

symbols.meaning: state vector; coordinates of the point representing the system in state space

symbols.dimensions: R x R^n x R^m -> R^n
R x R^n x R^m -> R^p

properties.property: The state variables span a geometric space, the state space (equivalently, time-domain approach, or phase space for certain dynamical systems), whose axes are the state variables; the system's instantaneous state is a point in this space given by the state vector.
properties.why: this is how the representation is defined before any matrix specialization

properties.property: For linear, time-invariant, finite-dimensional systems the state and output equations can be written in the compact matrix form ẋ(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t), y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t), giving an algebraic alternative to Laplace-transform frequency-domain analysis and extending naturally to multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems.
properties.why: matrix form is the LTI specialization of the general representation

properties.property: Unlike the frequency-domain (transfer-function) approach, the state-space representation is not restricted to linear systems with zero initial conditions.
properties.why: distinguishes the scope of state-space models from transfer-function methods

properties.property: In the general nonlinear form ẋ(t)=f(t,x(t),u(t)), y(t)=h(t,x(t),u(t)), the u(t) argument may be dropped when the system is unforced (has no inputs).
properties.why: shown explicitly as a stated simplification of the general form

properties.property: The matrix D encodes direct feedthrough from input to output; a strictly proper transfer function has D=0, while a proper (non-strictly-proper) transfer function has D=G(∞), a nonzero constant term added to the strictly proper part.
properties.why: identifies what the feedthrough matrix D represents in the state-space object

assumptions.assumption: Matrix form ẋ=Ax+Bu, y=Cx+Du requires the system to be linear, time-invariant, and finite-dimensional.
assumptions.breaks_when: the system is nonlinear, time-varying, or infinite-dimensional, in which case only the general f,h form applies

failure_modes.mode: Using the LTI matrix form to represent a system whose state equation is not a linear combination of states and inputs
failure_modes.signature: predicted trajectories from Ax+Bu diverge from the actual nonlinear dynamics (e.g. a pendulum's sin θ term cannot be captured by a constant A)
failure_modes.cause: f(t,x(t),u(t)) is nonlinear in x or u, so it cannot be reduced to A x + B u
